pitch_detail.notes: Powers over a bulging white roof, then on to gently overhanging or vertical crimping with assorted pockets and edges. The belay is a big ledge. The pitch works as a stand-alone single-pitch route.
Straight up dark rock on jugs. Can be linked with the first pitch (13 bolts total) if you want one longer lead.
Climb the white and red bulges. Easy, though the bolts are a bit spread out.

Three bolts, then angle left to join the finish of the neighbouring route Dream Machine, followed by two more widely spaced bolts to the step across Cleft. The Dream Machine bolt is a little hard to spot from the third bolt.

review.changed: Wrote all four pitches with grades, lengths and bolt counts where stated. P4 bolts given in notes only (3, then 2 more).

pitch_detail.notes: Begins easily on the first line to the right of the cave, moving left above the cave onto sustained climbing. Brush past the black streak before heading back right to the anchor above the black bugle-shaped feature. An 80 m rope reaches the cave on rappel, but put a knot in the end.
An easy, short romp with solid holds. After clip one, drift left, and stop beneath the roof where the black streak runs.

pitch_detail.anchor: shared with Brap Machine Paradise third-pitch anchors
pitch_detail.notes: 7 or 8 bolts. The black streak is the line, going through the roof via pockets and the occasional jug; the final big hold can be full of water. Mantle over, clip a few more bolts, then shift left about 10 ft to the anchors that also serve pitch 3 of the neighbouring route.
Same as the final pitch of Brap Machine Paradise: three bolts, then left to meet the last 2-3 bolts of Dream Machine.

review.changed: Wrote all four pitches. P3 bolt count is 7 or 8 per text, so given in notes only.

pitch_detail.notes: Fun climbing up a juggy water runnel to a small headwall where the hardest move lies, then a short walk and a few last moves to the anchors. Belay on a good ledge by the mahogany tree.

Go around the corner left and use stemming and chimney moves in the slot gully. Crux is a small headwall after bridging a gap. A short walk follows (two further bolts) and a few more moves to the anchor, which Yippee Ki Yay also uses for its second pitch.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches. Each has two-bolt rap-ring anchors per protection section; P2 bolt count as stated (7) with two more clipped on the walk, given in notes.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on the steeper rock right of the slab to the first bolt. Vertical ground with huge huecos, jugs, pockets, sidepulls and underclings follows. Work into the right-hand corner, clip the ninth bolt and pull the upper bulge. Finish up an easy low-angle water gully, clipping two more bolts on the right wall to the anchors.

Walk, scramble and climb up a ramp that gets steeper and better as you go, ending in a fun stemming chimney. An extendable alpine draw helps at the last bolt below the anchors. Finish on a comfortable two-bolt ledge.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches with grades, lengths and bolt counts.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on the ice when it feels right (a snowy gully system leads in) and climb about 75 ft until the flow becomes noticeably steeper.
The steeper upper part of the flow, about 150 ft, to the top.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches (feet to metres). The snowy gully approach is described in the notes of pitch 1.

pitch_detail.notes: A lower-angle gully with occasional bulges, ending at a bolted boulder belay. After heavy snowfall the ice can be mostly buried, but it is an easy lead everyone in a group can take.
The best pitch: tall vertical pillars into a run of steep ramps. Good top-rope potential across the flow. An easier lower-angle line exists on the right.
After topping out pitch 2, trudge through snow and trees to another low-angle gully finishing in a 3 m vertical ice step.
Walk further through snow with a couple of short vertical ice steps to reach a wide, bulgy ice sheet.
A short but dead-vertical piece of ice seen through the trees. Beyond it a short bushwhack through dense woods leads to a mountaintop marsh.

review.changed: Wrote all five pitches. Descent is raps from trees and tat without a station-by-station list, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: A wide flow offering three lines of roughly WI3+ to WI4. Left: ramping ice steps, the easiest and most relaxed, ending where you turn hard right to the big belay tree. Middle: a tight, airy ice chimney. Right: more vertical ice to a bushy top-out.

The best pitch, with thick ice throughout. The right side is a continuous run of ice steps around WI3 to WI3+. The middle line has an engaging ice dihedral with stemming and a good rest. The left-hand wall is a sustained blue ice face of around WI4+ to WI5-. A dagger in the centre may form a WI5 pillar in good years. Descend by rappelling from the tree anchors down to the large tree atop pitch 1.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches with the line options; grades are given as options in the notes, none on the pitch. No lengths stated.

pitch_detail.notes: Ice at 75-80 degrees, up to a belay just under the steeper pillars.
The steep pillars.
Continue up to the trees above.

review.changed: Wrote three pitches from a short description; no lengths or grades per pitch. Descent: rappel the route, no stations listed.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb the WI3 ice ramp to the foot of a WI4 column, then take the dihedral line or the column itself for about 30-35 ft of pumpy ice. Belay at a slung tree. The approach snow gully gives several ways onto the ice.

Hidden above and behind the first pitch, with two variants. Left: a traverse across poorly protected technical moves to the hard ice section, then 10-12 m to the top. Right: an easier 7 m climb up ice steps. Belay in trees either way.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches; the two can be linked with rope drag management.

pitch_detail.notes: From a large tree, climb the slab left of a rotten groove straight to a ledge. Follow the arete crack until it pushes you left beneath an overhang, then traverse left to a belay ledge with two bolts.
Straight up 30 ft past five bolts to the left side of the arete, with a good stance at the last bolt. Traverse right around the arete and up a groove to a mossy ramp with a single-bolt belay.
Scramble up and right through a roof along the easiest line to the top of the south summit and a two-bolt belay.

review.changed: Wrote all three pitches. Descent: walk off over the bridge.

pitch_detail.notes: Mixed ice pillar. The first crux is just off the ground: a fragile detached pillar and finicky mixed moves. Belay from the top of the steep snowfield above the icicle.

If the ice above connects, go straight up. Otherwise go right through steep unconsolidated snow to a vertical mud chimney; the first gear is likely above it, about 80 ft out. The climbing is manageable and mud takes good axe placements. Very runout and a rope stretcher: be ready to simul-climb. Belay where possible.
Traverse left to a distinct small chimney holding a decent WI3- flow. Belay at its base to reduce drag.
Climb the ice in the chimney, then veer right at the top. Belay from pickets or whatever else you can find.
Go right around the corner, then straight up where possible to the spine at the foot of a spire on your left.
Steep snow to the summit ridge.

review.changed: Wrote all six pitches. No lengths stated except an ~80 ft run to first protection on P2.

pitch_detail.notes: Scramble over broken, irregular ground to a large flake that has a little elderberry growing from its left edge. Protection en route is sparse, but the flake takes good anchor gear.

The pitch wanders. Go straight up 10 m to the prominent diagonal crack, then up and right across the slab with sparse gear to a second crack heading up left; a fixed pin sits at the junction. Follow the left crack to the headwall steps, an optional belay. Then either traverse right under the short step to trees, or (recommended) go directly up the headwall to the trees atop the dome, with good protection. Runouts exist.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches; P2 can be split at the top of the zig-zag crack.

pitch_detail.notes: Start on the east side of the former Lanthrop Glacier at the base of the buttress. About 200 ft of easy slabs lead to the foot of a big system of right-facing dihedrals.
Climb the right-facing dihedral system for about 150 ft to a stance below a gully.
Follow the gully to its end, then a 5.7 crack for about 70 ft to a small ledge.
Up and right about 75 ft to a large slab, then up and left across it to a big ledge.
Scramble about 75 ft of easier ground, then traverse about 75 ft left to a great ledge.
Go up and left from the belay onto the prow of the buttress and stay on it for about 20 ft, then traverse right and climb another 50 ft to a ledge.
Up and right about 75 ft to lower-angle ground (5.5) that often holds snow or rotten ice early in the season and is dry, crumbly rock in late summer.
About 150 ft directly up the lower-angle buttress to a ledge.

Traverse left toward the steep, knobby headwall. Easy but essentially unprotectable: long pitons or a hammer and Specters can be driven into the conglomerate, otherwise expect 40+ ft of runout up and left into a wide gully.
Follow the rotten low-angle gully to the 'chicken out' ledge. Scramble the summit block by the standard south line and descend the West Ridge.

review.changed: Wrote 10 entries (1-6, 7-9, 10, 11, 12-13). Lengths in feet are in notes (not exact). Descent is by the West Ridge, no rappels.

pitch_detail.notes: Wanders up ramps and corners; it may be snow or neve rather than ice, and the lower part can be buried depending on conditions.

A short (about 15 ft) dihedral with strenuous mixed moves, then toward the skylight. One bolt is at the foot of the skylight section; above it, pull over the bulge, which is the crux, and emerge on the summit ridge. Protection is limited at both cruxes and varies with conditions.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches and a two-station rappel table (bollard, then the pin-and-cord station), both described in order.

rappel_detail.notes: Rappel tat on the ridge may be buried under rime, so a bollard can be used instead.
Existing station. Double 70 m ropes reach the base from here.

pitch_detail.notes: A slab ramp into jams to pull a roof, then easier climbing to the foot of the corner, where you build the anchor.
Press and grunt up the corner; two bolts protect the crux. The left arete goes at about 5.7, so avoid it for the real route. Climb to the two-bolt anchor.
Optional final pitch leading to a walk-off. The rock is chossy, so rappelling from the P2 anchor with a 70 m rope to the tree at the first anchor is advised instead.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches (P3 optional). Stored count is 2. Descent: rap with a 70 m rope to the tree at the P1 anchor; no stations listed.
review.other_findings: Stored pitches 2; text describes an optional third pitch of about 5.7.

pitch_detail.notes: Two variations. Left: standard WI3 that is steeper than it looks, joining the upper ramp. Right: a short ice or mixed section off the glacier, then a long ice traverse to join the left line. Then traverse hard left to the foot of the snow gully; the upper ramp is under 60 m away. If the leader runs the ramp out as far as the rope allows, one more pitch reaches the top of the cleaver. The belay is in the snow gully.
Snow up, then ice or mixed directly above. Where ice stops, traverse right on dry loose rock with big exposure to the left, then a short ice bit joins the top of a neighbouring route. Belay there.
Move up and left around a corner over snow and simple rock, crossing a few small ridges, and aim for where the Right Gully route ends.
A brief, easy lead over snow and crumbly rock reaches the snowfields above the Right Gully ice pitches. From here about 500 ft of snow, ice and easy mixed leads to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 4 pitches with lengths. Beyond P4 the route continues about 500 vertical feet of snow, ice and easy mixed to the summit, noted in P4.

pitch_detail.notes: Cross the creek on ice bridges and stay above the spray zone to remain dry, using the highest line, with some technical downclimbing and traversing to the sheltered bolted belay. Soloing would be risky because a fall into the spray cone may not be survivable.

Descend slightly left from the belay, then traverse left about 40 ft behind the falls (runout). Use a pulley carabiner at the first bolt to reduce drag. Pull on spray-ice petals into an overhang, traverse right to a rest under the dagger, then clear the curtain and climb about 60 ft of WI5/6 past chandelier overhangs. Above the last ice roof it eases to a dry belay out right. Needs cold, well-bonded ice. Six screws plus 11 bolts.
Left on ice petals, optionally using a .5 cam in an iced block. Chimney against the ice shell, clip four bolts out right, pull the short overhang and top out on frozen turf. Belay from big trees.

review.changed: Wrote all three pitches with grades, lengths, bolts. No rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: The spray cone: interesting early season and nearly a walk later. Belay anyway, as a fall into the cone would be serious. Move quickly. The bolted station can be hard to find late. Protect with screws or, in thin ice, pecker/Specter pieces in turf. A half rope keeps the main rope dry.

The Cave. Short iced dihedrals, then a long, steady overhang of 30 to 40 degrees, working rightward as it rises. About 16 bolts (12-14 to reach the dagger) and optionally 1-2 screws on the final slab. Pre-hang long draws against rope drag. Footholds are plentiful and frozen moss gives placements.

The Thread. Right on mixed ground past the old belay, then stem between the ice thread and the steep rock, clipping bolts out left. Either 5 bolts or 4-8 screws depending on conditions. Grade depends on conditions; the ice may be only a few inches wide.

review.changed: Wrote all three pitches; bolt counts approximate, given in notes.

pitch_detail.notes: Spray traverse, same as the first pitch of Fennesz.

Belay safely inside the little cave under the rooflet, particularly if spray ice is above. Stem around the dagger on the right, which may not be connected: safe once the bolts begin, though exciting before that. Reach an overhanging dihedral with turf placements; the climbing is a sustained pump on poor feet, and the crux is the transfer onto the Fennesz dagger.
The top-out of Fennesz, as for the third pitch there.

review.changed: Wrote all three pitches; P1 and P3 identical to Fennesz.

skip_reasons.or_h_mt_thielsen_east_face_aka_brainless: Text is a hedged, condition-specific narrative of one ascent with approximate grades; no usable per-pitch beta.
